text:
Clinics rarely have high ratings, because when people are dissatisfied—especially in a vulnerable state—they almost always leave a negative review. But when everything goes well, most just pass by and forget. While I was in this hospital, I kept thinking about how underrated the doctors’ work is: day and night they save lives, run examinations, provide help, and still remain kind and attentive. To me, that is an act of true heroism.

I want to share my experience. At another clinic, I was given a wrong diagnosis—food poisoning. Medications and painkillers didn’t help. Appendicitis was suspected. I came here at 7 p.m. to the emergency department. They admitted me immediately, ran all the tests, and despite many patients (including accident victims and burn cases), they soon sent me for a CT scan, which confirmed the diagnosis. Before that, I was given IVs, and they constantly checked my pulse, blood pressure, and temperature.

The hospital has very modern, high-quality equipment, even though it is public. Before surgery, a woman came up to me, held my hand, and said: “Now I am responsible for you. You are safe with me. I will make sure everything goes perfectly.” In that moment—facing severe pain and pre-surgery anxiety—that reassurance meant the world to me. Thanks to her, I went into the operation completely calm.

The surgery went well, the wound was carefully stitched, and afterwards I was transferred to a ward. I spent a day in a private room with a beautiful view and very attentive care from the nurses. They were kind, many spoke English, constantly checked on me, changed IV lines, and helped with any request, even getting up to the bathroom. The food was surprisingly good for a hospital: shrimp soup, rice porridge with meat, little omelets.

The doctor encouraged me to get up and walk right away to avoid adhesions. Just 36 hours after surgery, I was discharged, since they follow modern protocols and don’t keep patients longer than necessary. They used waterproof dressings, so I could take a shower. After that, I was prescribed oral medication and outpatient dressing changes.

Now it’s the fifth day after the surgery, and I feel well. Unfortunately, I don’t know the names of the people who saved my life, but I am endlessly grateful to each of them for their dedication and care.

P.S. The view was amazing

text: I went to this hospital yesterday for mysterious bite. It’s a bit confusing where to go due to construction, parts of the hospital being closed, and signs being small and sparse, but just ask any staff and they point you to where you need to go, so it’s no problem. You have to talk to quite a lot of staff from start to finish, but overall the process was quite smooth and adequately explained. I spent slightly over an hour there, including a 30 minute observation period post injection. So not bad all things considered. Medical care was good. The reason I’m giving this hospital a five star overall is because they called to check up on my condition the following evening, and the lady on the phone was so sweet and caring. It felt highly personalized, which was so refreshing. Hope they keep the good service.

text: Unfortunately, I had to contact my insurance company. My 12-year-old child was poisoned. The diarrhea and vomiting stopped, but then his temperature rose. Halyk Bank, the insurance company, referred me to this hospital; it's quite a long …

It was a very positive experience. It was the first time in many years that I applied for insurance, and everything went extremely quickly and very pleasantly. The doctor examined me, prescribed treatment, and immediately gave me all the necessary medications. I also had some tests done, which took about an hour and a half to get.
P.S. One thing to keep in mind: they don't have an ophthalmologist.

This is a large hospital with not many patients, but the service is extremely slow. On September 24th, 2025, I came for a back abscess drainage procedure. After the examination, the doctor told me I needed surgery in the emergency room. I left the examination room at 2:04 PM. There was no indication that I was waiting for documents or for them to be sent to the examination room. I went to the emergency room and waited, but it took a very long time. I went to the counter and asked if my case had been sent to the emergency room. The staff at the counter asked for my name, and when I gave it, they said, "Oh, this person?" They were very unenthusiastic and slow. It took forever to get the documents sent to the emergency room. A staff member or nurse (I'm not sure) said I had to wait 1 to 2 hours because there were emergency cases. I would like to suggest that the hospital improve its service speed.

I'm not sure if there's any training for staff here about closing the examination room door or entering and exiting. I was examining the doctor in the room, with my clothes off, but the staff just opened the door and walked in and out without a hitch, without asking any questions. Not to mention, they didn't even close the door. There were people sitting in front of the room, so there was no privacy at all.
I wouldn't recommend this place to anyone. The only positive is the polite staff. …

T-Bank Insurance assigned me to this clinic when I applied, and it took me 40 minutes to get there by car.
Everything was organized inside: they took my medical history and documents right at the entrance, and gave me a ticket with directions to the 5th floor.
On that floor, they assigned me to a staff member, scanned my passport and insurance card, and waited about 30 minutes for them to test me for COVID and flu.
After the test, I waited about 2:30 for the results. Based on the test results, the doctor examined me and prescribed medication. The assigned person collected my medications about 30 minutes after the examination. I didn't have to pay on the spot; my T-Bank insurance allows direct payments (the bill was 5,100 baht) (the bank manager was always in touch and coordinated everything). Overall, everything was very convenient, but the wait time was extremely long. I arrived at 9:50 AM and left at 2:00 PM (there were no lines). The staff was polite and helpful. Special thanks to T-insurance for having good clinics as partners.

I brought my mother here, from when there were few people until it was crowded, and she still hasn't been tested. I'm confused about what kind of system they have. We sat waiting for 3-4 hours, and her fever started to flare up again. I'm going crazy.

A very good hospital! The service is fast and efficient. The staff is professional, and everything is done with care and attention. We used Halyk insurance, and everything went smoothly. The center is open 24/7, which is very convenient.
Salam aleikum from Kazakhstan! 🌍🇰🇿 …

This government-run hospital, affiliated with the Provincial Administrative Organization, offers services comparable to private hospitals. The doctors are very thorough in their examinations and explain things well to patients (general practitioners). The system is efficient, eliminating the need for long waits like in typical public hospitals. There's a restaurant on the 3rd floor.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, entry to the building was very strict. The parking lot is spacious and ample (most public hospitals nationwide have 100% parking problems, but this one doesn't). There's a convenience store, making it easy to buy goods and food. The staff provides excellent service.

They're incredibly sloppy. I went to the hospital and told them I'd be using accident insurance. They said okay. But when I got to the emergency room, another nurse said I had social security insurance at another hospital. I told them I wanted to use accident insurance, and they said, "Why didn't you tell me that earlier? You might have to pay upfront." Seriously? I told the first person, but they didn't even bother to communicate? This has happened twice now at this hospital. Please communicate with each other! Do you have a group chat on LINE?

I'd like to know what time the dental appointment queue closes. Last time I went, the queue was full. The nurse told me to come at 7 am. When I arrived at 7 am, they said the queue was full. I took time off work to come for service, but it was all for nothing. It's terrible.

text:
My wife has had a cough, sore throat, and phlegm for three days. At 5 a.m., we decided to go to the hospital. Tinkoff Insurance sent us to this hospital (it turned out to be a long way). We arrived at the hospital around 6:30 a.m. While we were figuring out what was going on, at 7:30 a.m., a nurse gave us plane number 1 and told us to wait for the doctor until 9:00 a.m. We spent an hour and a half sitting outside on chairs. A young doctor came, gave us a quick examination, and sent us to wait for a prescription. About 15 minutes later, Mrs. Maxim, the doctor, took us to the 5th floor of the hospital, asked us to email her the insurance policy, and then sat us down again. About 15 minutes later, my wife returned, we signed the paperwork, and we were given 4-5 packets of pills. It seemed fine, but it took a very long time. If we hadn't arrived in the morning, we would have spent another hour or more in line...
It seems like it's a paid appointment...
We don't have to wait for paid appointments.

Refuse if offered. Never come here. They sat with a baby for an hour waiting, then examined our children in a cold room with fevers for an hour. They barely persuaded us to take blood from our older daughter, ignored our questions, and then sent us to the hospital for three days.
Now the saddest thing is that they prescribed a bunch of medications for our older daughter, including an antibiotic, even though her test results were good. When we asked why and for what reason they prescribed the antibiotic, they pretended not to understand. On the last day, they disconnected the baby's IV literally five minutes after they brought the medication. When we asked why they brought it, they told us the senior doctor ordered it, and we followed it. We later realized she did it so they could send us home quickly, even though we hadn't asked for anything, as it was important to us that our child fully recovered. They didn't treat our older daughter at all. Tinkoff sent us here.

I don't recommend anyone go here. My child has rotavirus, and they made me wait in line for three hours because the doctor was on lunch break. When he arrived, he said, "Come back the next day for tests." Don't waste your time.

A cautionary tale for all patients: The nurses were excellent, but the female doctor in the emergency room on the night of March 9, 2025, Dr. Nuchada Khontai (fair-skinned, plump, Chinese-looking), was terrible. The nurse said she wasn't a resident doctor and only came occasionally. Everyone who encounters this doctor is pitiful. She was awful. She told a patient with diarrhea from a rotavirus infection that it might be colon cancer and refused to admit the patient, even though the patient had diarrhea for six consecutive days, almost 60 times, and was losing their balance due to severe dehydration. The doctor used many inappropriate words directed at a patient, even ignoring the patient's relatives standing beside them. She even brought up politics in the conversation. Doctor, if you're not ready to be a doctor, please resign. I understand you're tired and don't get enough rest, but do you know that the patients who come for emergency treatment are genuinely unwell and need your help? If they had a choice, they wouldn't want to come to the hospital. But you generalized and spoke in a way that people would call "disgusting." You have absolutely no medical ethics. And your medical school education is expensive! It takes many years to graduate, but it's unfortunate that doctors don't learn psychology and how to communicate with patients. If a doctor isn't ready to examine a patient, they should tell the hospital director. The director can then find staff who are more compassionate. Most importantly, if a doctor hasn't clearly diagnosed the illness, please don't speak to a patient like that; it can cause shock. No matter the patient's age, every life is precious. It's a shame that a doctor lacks courtesy and professionalism. Ultimately, they allowed the patient to stay in the hospital because we, the patient's family, insisted. Even though the blood test results were normal, the patient was very weak, barely able to stand. The doctor still couldn't figure it out and said he didn't want problems with the family. Finally, the hospital diagnosed the patient with rotavirus, requiring four days of intravenous fluids and treatment. If we had listened to the doctor that day, we would have sent the patient home. The patient only drank electrolyte solution, went to the bathroom more than ten times a day, couldn't eat anything, and vomited everything out. The patient would surely have gone into shock at home. (From a family who actually took the patient for treatment.) And I feel really bad.

P.S. If the doctor is tired and not in the mood to see patients, the doctor should write on the emergency room door on the days they are on duty: "Do not get sick while the doctor is on duty." That way, patients will understand. Thank you.

Don't come here outside of business hours. The doctor is unwilling to treat you. I had a severe cough at night and came to see him. He just said there was no pus in my throat and told me to take the medicine home. He didn't even let me …

Terrible. The screening process is slow, people are sitting around playing on their phones, so clumsy. The pharmacy counter is only one counter with a huge queue. They really need to improve this. Patients could die from the wait!
